articles.title: EA Sports FC 27 Review So Far
articles.summary: EA Sports stands on shaky ground with a new open-world hub, but the realistic, intuitive Tactics system shows promise.
articles.body:
I find myself in a weird place for my in-progress review of EA Sports FC 27. On one hand, worthwhile strategic elements have finally been added that reflect real-world tactics in a concise, intuitive way. On the other hand, the promised improvements to behavior and pathing of computer-controlled players on the field still ring hollow, carrying over many of the same issues the series has had for over a decade. Couple this with the dreaded introduction of open-world elements via The Grounds, and the result is yet another instance of positive steps forward but negative steps backward.

Ever since NBA 2K14 introduced MyPark, which eventually evolved into The Neighborhood in NBA 2K18 and The City in NBA 2K21, I figured it was only a matter of time before EA brought a similar open world full of activities to its sports franchises. While The Grounds isn't without merit, it often feels like EA is trying to solve a problem that didn't really exist.

My first impression is that The Grounds doesn’t need to be an open-world environment to deliver what the playerbase wants out of a more communal online mode. I don’t need to run through a visually saturated, low-resolution city populated by lifeless NPCs just to find a game mode to start up when simple menus devoted to the same function can do the same thing in a more efficient manner. Sure, it works well as an active lobby for matchmaking and makes it easier to find other players and move between activities, but between the framerate drops and unnatural character animations, nothing immersed me in the hub in EA Sports FC 27 enough to justify its existence.

The issues above are only compounded by the myriad of unskippable cutscenes and NBA 2K15-level voice acting that make up The Grounds. The irony is that I was initially excited by the new hub world because it brings back one of my favorite FIFA characters from The Journey story mode: Alex Hunter, who first appeared in FIFA 17 and FIFA 18, once again voiced by Adetomiwa Edun. That enthusiasm disappeared quickly once Hunter began speaking, as his delivery feels noticeably more rigid and detached than it did during his original story.

Edun's performance nearly a decade ago was passionate and natural, whereas The Grounds' version of Hunter sounds like he would rather be anywhere else. Things get even more painful when Kylian Mbappe appears shortly afterward, delivering his lines with such a stiff, mechanical cadence that it was clear he read his lines directly from a script all in one take. I honestly found myself grateful that my created character doesn't speak to avoid adding more uncomfortable interactions. While I plan to explore more of the online portion of The Grounds this weekend, the hub itself has not made a particularly strong first impression.

When it comes to gameplay, EA Sports FC 27's expanded Tactics system is easily the best addition, wonderfully complementing the playstyles and roles introduced over the past few years. The new strategy system gives much more control over how teams behave in different phases of play, going beyond basic formations and instructions by explaining the purpose, strengths, and weaknesses of different tactical approaches. This becomes particularly useful when building around individual player attributes. As a Manchester United fan, I found that a deeper defensive approach worked especially well for Noussair Mazraoui, whose patient style lets him maintain his position and disrupt attacks without constantly stepping out of shape, while a short-passing buildup gives him chances to use his technical ability without abandoning that defensive structure.

That flexibility became even more apparent when I switched formations on the fly mid-match while playing against Crystal Palace – I found that they were leaving space along the wings, so I moved into a 4-2-2-2, letting Bruno Fernandes operate between the lines and thread passes to a striker such as Benjamin Sesko, creating opportunities for quick combinations and finishes through the middle. Alternatively, when I faced Manchester City, they controlled the wings more successfully. To counter this, I switched to a 4-2-3-1 wide formation, moving Fernandes more centrally so he dictates play and combines with holding midfielders such as Kobbie Mainoo through quick one-two passes.

Separating tactical instructions for possession and defensive phases adds another useful layer, while Player Roles give individual players more specific responsibilities within a formation. Instead of simply placing someone in a position and expecting them to behave a certain way, I can now build their role around the specific contribution I want from them. For example, if I move into a 4-2-3-1 wide and place Benjamin Šeško on the right side, I can adjust his role depending on the circumstances. As an inside forward, he can cut inward to create shooting opportunities or provide another passing option for Fernandes, while a wider role allows him to stretch the defense and open space through the middle.

That same flexibility can be useful defensively, particularly when protecting a lead. If an opponent repeatedly targets his side of the pitch, giving Šeško more defensive responsibility lets him drop back and support the right back, providing another way to protect that flank without abandoning the attacking structure. What makes the system particularly valuable is that it teaches the strategy behind soccer formations without overwhelming players with unnecessary information. EA Sports FC 27 does a good job explaining why different shapes work, which players suit them, and how to adjust them against different opponents, making the tactical aspect for the sport approachable while still leaving experienced players plenty of room to experiment.

The biggest issue is that the tactical system can sometimes feel like it is working against the game's own computer-controlled behavior. Pathing and defensive logic can still break down on higher difficulties, allowing a carefully constructed gameplan to be undermined by an CPU defender refusing to challenge for a 50/50 ball or making an inexplicable movement. Passing will still occasionally produce similarly frustrating results when a ball aimed toward an open teammate on the right is instead sent toward a covered player in the middle.

Crossing and corner kicks have also improved noticeably, with both systems producing more convincing positioning battles and giving the player greater control over what happens inside the box. I scored several successful headers with Harry Maguire from corners during my time with the game, which stood out because I could count on one hand the number of corner routines and headed goals I had scored in previous EA Sports FC entries.

I'm going to explore Career Mode, Presentation, Online, and Ultimate Team, and dive deeper into how Tactics will affect both single-player and multiplayer modes, in the coming days before locking in my full scored review – stay tuned.

articles.title: We Ranked the 10 Best First Partner Pokémon TCG Cards of All Time
articles.summary: We ranked the 10 best First Partner Pokémon TCG cards of all time, featuring $4,500 vintage grails, iconic Charizard classics, and budget-friendly picks.
articles.body:
With 2026 marking Pokémon’s milestone 30th Anniversary, what better way to celebrate than by taking a nostalgic stroll down memory lane with the ones who started our journeys?

Between the First Partner collection flying off the shelves quicker than a Regieleki and the simultaneous global drop of the 30th Anniversary expansion, our original First Partner Pokémon are dominating tabletop conversations like never before.

Venusaur & Snivy GX - SM229 - SM Promos (SMP)

Scorbunny — ME: Ascended Heroes #225/217

Torchic Star — EX Team Rocket Returns #108/109

Pikachu ex — ME: Ascended Heroes #276/217

No matter who your First Partner was, there’s a gorgeous card out there for you - here’s my list of the top 10 First Partner Pokémon cards of all time, ranked by artwork, affordability, and impact they’ve had.

Before we jump in, for those after 30th Celebration boosters, our best suggestion right now is to request an invite from Amazon for the ETB, at least , priced much more reasonably compared to other retailers. Invites will be sent out soon!

10. Primarina — ME05: Pitch Black #088/084

This is genuinely one of my favorite cards of all time, let alone First Partner Pokémon! While first-stage First Partner Pokémon usually get the Pyroar’s share of cute Illustration Rares, satoma’s work on this final stage Primarina from Pitch Black is class.

I love the golden sun, and its glittering beachy vibe that give Alola’s siren starter a spotlight worthy of a stage-performer. You can pick this up on TCGplayer for $4.49, making it a shockingly affordable piece of art.

9. Mudkip — ME: Mega Evolution Promo #057

This promo card from the First Partner lineup captures this water-type looking completely adorable. The artwork by Saboteri is crammed with subtle Gen 3 lore details in the background.

My first-ever Pokémon game was Pokémon Ruby, but my partner got me a 3DS for my 21st birthday where I finally completed my starter trio with Mudkip in Omega Ruby, so picking up this promo was a non-negotiable personal mission for me. Right now, it's holding steady at around $20.56 on TCGplayer.

8. Charizard (Classic Collection #4/102)

It had to be in here! The holy grail that arguably started this hobby all those years ago, Mitsuhiro Arita’s Base Set Charizard is the card that launched a million binder collections. The iconic Shadowless variant—lacking the dark drop shadow along the right border of the art box—remains the undisputed King of Nostalgia. Now, with the 30th Anniversary reprints, this card takes the crown as my favorite Charizard card because it gives more people a chance to own a slice of history.

A special shoutout goes to the 151 Charizard ex Special Illustration Rare as well, but I couldn't bring myself to put two Charizards on the list when there’s so many other First Partner Pokémon and art to celebrate! Unsurprisingly, market values on TCGplayer for the OG sit around $1,160 for raw copies, depending heavily on condition, but now more Trainers can get their hands on it thanks to the 30th Anniversary reprints, who knows what will happen. Have you managed to get your hands on one yet?

7. Piplup (Secret) - SM - Cosmic Eclipse (SM12)

Before Trainer Gallery cards became a main-set staple, Cosmic Eclipse gave us Dawn and Piplup in this adorable SIR. Tomomi Kaneko’s artwork highlights Sinnoh’s Dawn alongside her stubborn Piplup at the Canalave City docks. Because of its legendary status among Gen 4 fans, you’re looking at around $88.24 on TCGPlayer.

6. Venusaur & Snivy-GX — SM Promos #SM229

Yes, I know this card has two First Partners in it, but I’m strictly counting it as one entry! I have a lot of time for artist Yuka Morii, who hand-sculpts every featured Pokémon out of physical clay before photographing them in real-world outdoor dioramas.

When I went to EUIC in 2025, they had her original physical clay sculptures on display at the venue, and seeing the real-world scale and tactile craftsmanship behind the card in person was so unbelievably cool. If you want to add this gorgeous clay tag team to your collection, it's currently running around $146.63 on TCGPlayer.

5. Scorbunny — ME: Ascended Heroes #225/217

Veteran illustrator Yuu Nishida hit an absolute home run (wrong sport, but close enough) with this Galar First Partner. The artwork catches Scorbunny chilling out on a fresh bed of leaves.

Thankfully, this Fire-type doesn’t have any flames while resting. Best of all, it's super easy on the wallet, hovering at just $9.26 on TCGplayer.

When it comes to cozy charm, it doesn’t get much better than Tepig from Unova. Orca’s warm and golden lighting shows Tepig warming its belly, rolling around in a heap of crisp autumn leaves.

This calm, simple illustration makes you smile the moment you open the binder, and you can get a copy on TCGplayer for around $52.50.

3. Torchic Star — EX Team Rocket Returns #108/109

Generation 3 holds a massive place in my heart, and while the whole Gen 3 TCG era produced absolute bangers, this is easily my favorite piece in the entire collection.

Illustrated by Masakazu Fukuda, Gold Star cards had artwork that broke out of the frame. Sorry if your First Partner was Torchic though, copies of this card are ultra-rare and currently average around a wild $4,500.00 on LimitlessTCG.

2. Pikachu ex — ME: Ascended Heroes #276/217

Look, I know Pikachu is a bit of a rogue choice for a "First Partner" list compared to the standard Grass/Fire/Water trios, but let’s not forget Pokémon Yellow (and Let's Go, Pikachu!)! Pikachu was, arguably, our very first First Partner, so it absolutely earns a spot here.

USUMON’s ultra-high-contrast, electric-charged art style makes the iconic mascot practically leap off the foil, though pulling off that high-voltage style means it commands a heavy $935.99 market price on TCGplayer.

1. Greninja ex - 148/128 - ME: 30th Celebration

This card is just awesome. Everyone loves Greninja, but artist GIDORA completely stole the 30th Anniversary show with this one. Did you spot the Eevee and Lucario in the background?

Between the playful street-style vibe and the hype surrounding the set, this could easily be one of the most fun chase cards modern Pokémon has seen in a long time. Because it’s so new, the market is pretty volatile, currently sitting around $70.99 on TCGPlayer.

Sara Heritage is a freelance journalist for IGN, specialising in Pokémon TCG. When she's not gaming, you’ll probably find her building yet another LEGO set she absolutely did not need, or chaining ranked matches in Pokémon Champions.

articles.title: Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave - How to Recruit the Best Characters - IGN

articles.title: Resident Evil Fans 'Will Feel Seen' After the Movie, Says Director Zach Cregger
articles.summary: Resident Evil director Zach Cregger and star Austin Abrams sit down to delve into how they revived the beloved horror franchise on the big screen.
articles.body:
The Resident Evil movie reboot has finally arrived, coming from one of the biggest names in horror these days, filmmaker Zach Cregger, who previously wowed fans with his films Barbarian and Weapons . And he certainly seems to be off to a good start with Resident Evil -- we gave it an 8 out of 10 here at IGN, it's in the 90s on both the Rotten Tomatoes critics and audience scores, and it's on track to be a winner at the box office as well.

IGN's own Tom Jorgensen recently sat down with Cregger and the film's star Austin Abrams -- who plays Bryan, a medical courier with some serious bad luck -- to discuss the divided fan response to the film before it came out, how Cregger and his team went about evoking a true "video game feel" with the reboot, how Abrams almost got killed by a 150-pound bag of blood during production (!), and much more.

You can watch the discussion at the video above, or read it all right here...

Tom Jorgensen for IGN: There is a little bit of a conversation going on about this movie about to what degree it's staying faithful to the games.

Zach Cregger: A little bit of a conversation?

IGN: A tiny, little bit of a conversation.

ZC: Wow. Okay. That's putting it lightly.

IGN: Have there been unexpected challenges in convincing people this is the way to do this?

ZC: Yeah. I mean, of course. I think I was naive when I... I thought that fans of these games like me would be thrilled that somebody was coming along and turning Resident Evil into a survival horror movie. And I was like, “That's great.” I did not really appreciate the sentiment [of] “We've been waiting forever for Leon's story.” And I appreciate that. And I'm sorry that that's not the story that I'm bringing here. I mean, I get it. I understand the frustration.

I understand it so well because I haven't seen the earlier movies, because they don't look like the Resident Evil that I love. You know what I mean? So how could I be frustrated with fans who have that same attitude? My only hope is that they will see the movie regardless of their skepticism or their disappointment that I'm not telling some of the stories that the games tell so well, and that they will feel seen when they do watch the movie and they will recognize all of the love for the games that is in this movie because it is there. And this is not just me telling a story and slapping Resident Evil on it so I can get a budget. This is me telling a Resident Evil story. I understand the resistance. I really do, because I have it myself. But it is coming from a true place of love.

IGN: I think historically video game adaptations have really struggled to translate the active experience of playing a video game into more of a passive experience [of] watching a film. How did that inform your choice to lean a little bit away from the specifics of exactly what happens in the Resident Evil games and more into how it feels to play them?

ZC: Well, there's a lot of answers to that question. The first thing that comes to mind is the camera work. I'm using the language of the games in the camera work. So I'm staying rooted in that third-person, over the shoulder with a big wide lens [style], which is how all of these games are. That's their language. And so that was a really fun thing, is to just almost one-to-one the visual language of the games in there.

And then to utilize the pacing of the games, the survival horror, the dread, the journey on foot where you're entering this terrifying scenario, and you have two shotgun shells and you're wounded. And that is such a fun, loaded, cinematic element that the games have done so well since the beginning, but the movies don't really seem to be concerned with. And so I wanted to make a survival horror movie and pick up on all those things. I utilize the setting and the t-Virus and the Umbrella Corporation, all of those little ingredients that make Resident Evil, Resident Evil – that's the bedrock of this movie as well. Another aspect [is] the length of the games, like weapon progression, starting with a pistol, graduating to the shotgun, graduating to the MP5. The increasingly dangerous enemies and mutants that you encounter.

Austin Abrams: The language, too, that you were talking about, just the camera and the angles of figuring out that dance, especially if it is over the shoulder or something of where to move and have the [camera] operator... We're moving around and we're doing a lot of things in one take. So getting that choreography right, but also doing it in a way that feels…

AA: ...fresh and dynamic, was just another aspect to it that was tricky to do.

IGN: What conversations were you having with your DP and your camera department on this? Was it important that they have experienced and played the games, or were these conversations that you were able to have more on set just practically speaking in terms of how to achieve that look?

ZC: No, I don't need my camera department to have played the games. I'm the captain of what we see, so I'm going to make sure that we have the right lens and that we are moving correctly. So no, that's on me. They need to make sure it's lit well, but I'm the boss of how it moves and what lens is picked.

James is our camera operator who came straight from The Odyssey , where he was lugging that giant IMAX thing around. And so now he had a normal-size camera and he was able to be really agile with it. I think he felt really liberated. And he's played video games because most people in our age [group] and younger have grown up on video games. So we all fundamentally understand the visual language of these games. And so it was a fun challenge for him to anticipate his attention and get there in time and tag these data points together. It was a really cool thing and it feels game-like.

AA: And I'll say that's why I felt comfortable going into it, because I knew that [Zach] was so passionate about it and had played so many hours of it. So he really knew the language of the games, and so that he could really be the captain. And I mean he really was … being very clear with everyone like, “No, this is what needs to happen and this is what needs to happen.”

I think [he was] really protecting the games in that way and protecting especially how you feel while you're playing the games. … If it was someone else that wasn't as much of a fan, that wasn't as passionate about the games, I wouldn't have felt comfortable.

IGN: You mentioned in our breakdown of the first trailer that there's only two or three scenes in this movie that are really leaning into zombies or vanilla zombies. Why was that important to you for this movie to not really focus on zombies?

ZC: It's not that that was not important. As I was writing the story, it's just the story. I'm a big fan of letting the story tell itself to me, and this is the way the story naturally unfolded. I think I maybe shouldn't have said that, because I think there are more scenes than I mentioned that have zombies. I didn't expect people to really grab onto that as a bad thing. You don't know what the other things are, so how can you get mad at this yet? The t-Virus is more interesting than just zombies. You know what I mean? The t-Virus can do all sorts of fascinating things with organic matter. So why would I not utilize that as much as possible? So I'm surprised that I have as many scenes as I do where zombies are just zombies.

IGN: Austin, you're playing a character original to this world. You're getting to start from scratch on that. Was that freeing for you, knowing that you didn't have to live up to some specific expectation from the game?

AA: Yeah, definitely … because it makes it so that you can go any direction. So we could really just come up with whatever was feeling right, and what felt also the most interesting to watch. I feel like a more interesting person to watch go through this experience is someone that doesn't know what they're doing, and also just wants the best almost for everyone and is a good-hearted person that then has to face all of these horrors. To me, [that] felt like a fun thing to watch.

IGN: Were there any other horror movie performances that you looked to for inspiration and how to build Brian and how capable he is in this world?

AA: I'm not sure. There wasn't necessarily horror movie inspirations, but there was... I think we found as we were going that there were character inspirations. And we've talked about this, but one being Marty McFly a little bit, and then Kevin McCallister and then John McClane…

AA: …and oscillating between the three of those guys. So that did become an inspiration. But I wouldn't say earlier on that there was necessarily a horror movie inspiration. But definitely more in the vein of the person that is just ill-equipped to deal with it, which just makes it more fun I think for everyone.

IGN: Because your previous films have messed a little bit with narrative structure and moved things around a little bit, what new challenges as a director did you run into in maintaining one thread of momentum right through to the end? And then, Austin, how do you support that in your performance? How do you shoulder all that momentum?

ZC: I mean the answer's in the question, right? It's like, is it possible to make a movie that is adrenalized for 85% of the movie? There are a couple of moments of little lulls here and there, but really, this movie is like tension, release, tension, release, tension, release. Can you stick with that for the runtime? That is a unique challenge. Weapons or Barbarian have their moments, but they also have all these story-building lulls in there that I love. But this movie, the goal in the challenge was “Let's floor it and let's never stop flooring it.” And that was hard. Hard on you.

AA: Yeah. Well, and the aspect of that too is keeping in mind like, “Okay, where am I right now in this journey? Am I starting to get a little bit more comfortable maybe with the weapons or am I…” Because you're having all these reactions to these crazy things, and it's just doing your best to make them all feel unique, but also feel like there's a progression here, especially when it's like, “Okay, well I've been surprised by a ton of monsters,” so it's like, “Can we do this in a new way or is it still hitting me in the same way, or am I a little bit more used to it now?”

ZC: You have to be cognizant that you're not just doing the same thing over and over. We need to build an arc into it. And that's hard when everything that keeps happening is like level 10. But, I think he did.

IGN: My favorite story that I have heard from the set of this film so far is that during the zombies off the roof scene, Austin, you were nearly taken out by a 150-pound bag of blood, I believe. Did you clock that in the moment as you were running or was that like a, “Hey, you got to come to playback and check something out, dude.”

AA: I remember running and then being like, “Oh, whoa, that was close.” But I kept to my line and thankfully there weren't any slips or anything like that. And then afterwards people being like, “Oh dude, that was…”

ZC: I remember bringing him to the monitor and being like, “Watch this.”

IGN: Can either of you remember the first time in your life that you really truly had the shit scared out of you by a video game?

AA: I feel like I was playing Dead Space, I think. I remember that just really... I think I tried playing it, and I just couldn't make it through it actually. Yeah, it just really freaked me out.

ZC: Not the first time, but the most effective was Resident Evil 8. I played in VR, and that baby in the basement. It actually scared me so bad I had to stop. And I don't think I've ever noped out of anything as an adult, but that did it. … In VR, dude, it was too intense.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

articles.title: Lollipop Chainsaw Live-Action Movie Revealed by Dragami Games
articles.summary: A live-action Lollipop Chainsaw movie is officially in the works, developer Dragami Games has announced.
articles.body:
A live-action Lollipop Chainsaw movie is officially in the works, developer Dragami Games has announced.

The studio behind the series revival announced plans to bring Juliet Starling to the big screen as part of Tokyo Game Show 2026, with full details shared by Deadline . It's yet another addition to the series as Dragami moves ahead with other previously announced installments, including an anime series and video game sequel .

The Lollipop Chainsaw movie will tell a prequel story set before the events of developer Grasshopper Manufacture's original bubblegum action game. It's also aimed to be an "R-rated action comedy" and will, once again, follow Juliet as the main character. Deadline also shared a brief story synopsis: "When a catastrophic zombie outbreak engulfs her school, Juliet must fight her way through the undead to save her friends, protect her family, and somehow keep her boyfriend Nick close – even if doing so ultimately requires some highly unconventional arrangements."

Dragami's film is said to be in development from an "international creative and production team" that includes Nada Holdings' Joe Teng, former ZDF Studios drama boss Robert Franke, Throne Inc MD Takafumi Yuki, Ambitious Entertainment's Kirk Shaw, and Non Stop TV's Patricio Rabuffetti. There is no word on whether original team members like Suda51 or now-DC Studios co-CEO James Gunn are involved, suggesting that, at least at this stage, they aren't attached in any capacity.

"We are truly excited to see our vision take another important step with the franchise’s first live-action feature film," Dragami president Shohei Sato said. "We are especially pleased to be working with such an experienced and passionate international team — one that understands what makes Lollipop Chainsaw special while embracing the opportunity to create something new."

Lollipop Chainsaw has been on a bit of a tear despite largely straying from the public eye for the last decade or so. Although it's firmly kept its place as a cult classic and fan-favorite Suda51 game, it wasn't until Dragami announced its RePop remaster in 2022 that Juliet started to turn heads once again. Whether an attempt to reanimate the franchise will succeed remains to be seen, though.

Upcoming New Video Game Movies and TV Shows: 2026 Release Dates and Beyond

After RePop finally launched in 2024, Dragami announced plans to continue the series with new installments in the near future. The most recent peek at what exactly that entails actually arrived earlier this week with the reveal of Lollipop Chainsaw 2 Back2Back . First gameplay has revealed a project that looks both familiar and extremely different, leaving fans hesitant to see can stick the landing without Suda51 or Gunn's help.

The announcement that a Lollipop Chainsaw movie has encouraged similar responses from fans. For now, no information about the project's cast or release date has been revealed.

"We are making a film that feels unmistakably true to the spirit of Lollipop Chainsaw while standing completely on its own," Franke said. "Longtime fans will recognize the attitude, irreverence, and glorious excess they love, while newcomers can simply enjoy an unforgettable action-horror comedy. Our ambition is to create a film that entertains audiences everywhere, whether they’ve played the game or not."

It looks like we've got some waiting to do while Dragami revs up its Lollipop Chainsaw movie. Until then, you can read IGN's 5/10 review for the original game, where we said it "doesn’t even attempt to differentiate itself from the genre, and most of what it does try new in the realm of its characters and writing ultimately ends up taking away from an incredible-on-paper action game.

"The music and sidekick are really all you can rely on to stay great from start to finish. The rest of Lollipop Chainsaw is all over the place before it ultimately settles for mediocrity and disappointment."

Michael Cripe is a freelance writer with IGN. He's best known for his work at sites like The Pitch, The Escapist, and OnlySP. Be sure to give him a follow on Bluesky (@mikecripe.bsky.social) and Twitter (@MikeCripe).

articles.title: Marvel's Wolverine Developer Nerfs Scent Trails and Audio Sense Indicators After 'Fart Gas' Backlash
articles.summary: Insomniac has released an update for Marvel’s Wolverine that nerfs the “fart gas” that had become such a talking point even before the game’s release.
articles.body:
Insomniac has released an update for Marvel’s Wolverine that nerfs the “fart gas” that had become such a talking point even before the game’s release.

The debate around this was rekindled following the publication of Marvel’s Wolverine reviews earlier this month, with The Washington Post journalist Gene Park calling the scent trail “fart gas” because of the way it appears behind characters Logan follows.

Jean Grey’s fart gas trail is NOT part of the navigation assist option. i turned it on and there’s another green line that tells you where to go. mission waypoint (yellow marker) is on as well and THAT can be turned off. 2nd pic i turn off the options and the gas stays. it seems… pic.twitter.com/cKs9uTPSG0 — Gene Park (@GenePark) September 10, 2026

Jean Grey’s fart gas trail is NOT part of the navigation assist option. i turned it on and there’s another green line that tells you where to go. mission waypoint (yellow marker) is on as well and THAT can be turned off. 2nd pic i turn off the options and the gas stays. it seems… pic.twitter.com/cKs9uTPSG0

There was some confusion online about the ability to turn this feature off via accessibility options. Insomniac’s official list of accessibility options for Wolverine includes a “Chase Assist,” which lets you toggle reduced movement speed for targets during chase sequences, but it does not turn off the trail. Other navigation toggles do not turn off the scent trail either.

Ahead of Wolverine’s release, Insomniac’s director of community and marketing, James Stevenson, took to social media to explain that Logan's scent trail is baked into the way the mutant's powers work.

“The scent trail isn’t always on,” he clarified. “It represents Logan’s canon mutant super senses and elite tracking ability. It only is there when he’s tracking a specific scent / sound (a person, whisky, or another clue scent) - story/mission moments or when he catches whiff of a collectible.”

Referencing previous discourse about Final Fantasy’s yellow paint guides , some have said Logan's scent trails remove any potential skill required for chase sequences and any joy of discovery in exploration.

Then, earlier this week, Insomniac said it was planning to “further refine the player experience” based on feedback , while insisting it’s “incredibly proud” of the game. Most took that to mean it intended to tweak the “fart gas,” and so it has proved.

The patch notes, posted to Insomniac’s website , confirms the hotfix “adjusts the presentation of the Scent Trails and Audio Sense indicators, including reduced opacity to make these visuals less intense.”

So, the “fart gas” will feel less in your face from now on. But there’s more. Insomniac said it’s exploring adding toggleable options for a future update, which suggests players may eventually be able to turn off Scent Trails completely. Patch notes are below.

Marvel’s Wolverine update v.01.001.005 patch notes:

This hotfix addresses some common crashes experienced by a small percentage of players since launch.

Additionally, this hotfix adjusts the presentation of the Scent Trails and Audio Sense indicators, including reduced opacity to make these visuals less intense.

Our team continues to evaluate ways to further improve Senses in the game, including exploring toggleable options for a future update.

articles.title: As Fans Flood the World of Warcraft: Forever Beta, Dev Says It's Putting Up 'The Craziest Numbers I've Seen in 17 Years Working at Blizzard'
articles.summary: World of Warcraft: Forever looks like it could be a smash hit after the launch of the beta was overrun with eager fans, surprising even Blizzard itself.
articles.body:
World of Warcraft: Forever looks like it could be a smash hit after the launch of the beta was overrun with eager fans, surprising even Blizzard itself.

Blizzard’s ended last weekend’s BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremony with the announcement of World of Warcraft: Forever , a “Classic Plus” MMO developed by the World of Warcraft Classic team, and set during the first year of World of Warcraft.

While Forever doesn’t launch until November 4, the beta was made available this week, and it was flooded by players. Those who did manage to get in faced disconnects. And then actually playing the game was tough due to extreme lag with looting and accepting quests. Hardly ideal.

World of Warcraft Classic developer Josh Greenfield took to X / Twitter to provide some insight into the popularity of the beta.

“Man, it was hard to sleep last night, I was so excited,” Greenfield said. “Beta has been... crazy. The craziest numbers I've seen in 17 years working at Blizzard and almost eight years on classic.

“We've got something really special here.”

That suggests significant interest in Forever, beyond even the launch of Classic itself. As a grizzled veteran of World of Warcraft’s early years, I remember well the brutal login queues most players would face when the groundbreaking MMO launched late 2004 and early 2005. Forever is rekindling those memories for me.

So, what’s going on with those queues? World of Warcraft senior game producer Tom Ellis took to X / Twitter to offer an explanation that acts as a fascinating insight into what goes on with the launch of an MMO. The upshot is this is a beta, and usually World of Warcraft betas don’t see this sort of interest.

“AHMAGERD, this game is 20 years old, how do you still suck at this!?! a. Heh, fair enough, short answer is, this is our BETA PTR environment stack, it's not a Production stack by a long, long, long, long, long, long shot. Betas for WoW aren't usually huge meter movers so this environment just isn't that powerful. This led to the first problem you saw today,” Ellis explained.

If you’ve got even a casual interest in online game infrastructure, Ellis’ post is worth a read. Ultimately, though, Blizzard sorted out the problems and the Forever beta is now running smoothly.

“Marked live once again and you all poured in without fuss,” he said. “Right now things are incredibly smooth for the first few hours of a public beta, Classic teams watching and fixing anything blocking that comes up but we're otherwise pretty much done for the night, enjoy!”

And that's what players are doing. I've seen multiple posts from fans praising the new visuals (in particular, the improved lighting), new sound effects (that rain!), and, from those who were there back in the day, the nostalgia-fueled trip down memory lane.

articles.title: The Blood of Dawnwalker Modders Aren’t Missing the Point – They Just Love the Game
articles.summary: Modders are extending The Blood of Dawnwalker's 30-day time limit to allow more time to complete every questline. But while this goes against the developer's vision, it shouldn't be seen as vandalism.
articles.body:
This is an IGN opinion piece from Mat Jones, who thinks everyone’s made too big a deal out of experience-altering mods, and wouldn’t replay a video game ever, even if he were forced to do so by vampires holding his family hostage.

I’ve spent the weeks since The Blood of Dawnwalker’s release nodding at headlines about how the time-pressured quest to rescue lead character Coen’s family – which is on a controversial 30-day timer – is the heart of the design, and that anyone looking to extend that clock with a mod wouldn’t be having the intended experience .

But, after reading that the developers themselves aren’t so bothered about the timer that they’d definitely want to add it in again – that a Dawnwalker sequel could strip out this mechanic and still inexorably be a Dawnwalker game – I’ve interrogated my own assumptions. I wonder if we’ve been giving anyone who’d roll back a couple of 0s on the odometer too hard a ride. Is the example of the “irresponsible modder”, someone incapable of understanding that developer intent should supersede any possible alteration, a fantasy?

The threat of a ticking clock is one of the first things you learn in screen writing classes: that a scene is more tense if there’s an outside force driving it forward, that a conversation which would otherwise just be two people in a room is twice as interesting if one of them really needs to get out of there. In a movie it's contrivance; obviously the timer can’t end until it’s dramatically interesting. A game, meanwhile, has to account for your character learning they’re about to explode and then just doing their idle animation for their remaining twenty minutes of life. The idea of a long-tail timer achieves the same aim as the movie version, though. Every decision matters if you can only make so many of them, and everything has more weight if there’s a cost.

It’s unlikely that Dawnwalker’s modders, or any modders who’d take the time limit out of any game, are unaware of this. I’m cynical about trends, I’m not cynical about individual people. I can imagine someone who has reckoned with this decision has thought about why these systems are implemented, but eventually accepts their “vandalism” of the art as a small price to pay to overcome problems inherent to this scale of game design.

Many games don’t benefit from a second playthrough. I’ve been playing games almost daily for over thirty years. I’m more than aware of how much gristle and sinew there is among the meat. I’ve chosen not to go back to a lot of things that I’ve loved in the past because I haven’t wanted to do the same stuff over and over. For every great bit of combat design in the best open world games, for every narrative twist and turn, there’s a lot of looking around in cupboards for bullets or pissing around in menus trying on new shoelaces that give you an extra 3% poison damage. Dawnwalker is no different; the equipment variety that will help in the quest to defeat the story’s vampiric villain, Brencis, is as incremental in scale as any other game. I’m fine doing this sort of stuff the first go through, but when I’ve absorbed the majority of the experience, it’s a challenge to get myself to care again.

If there’s, say, enough unique stuff in Dawnwalker for a player to only see 70 or 80% of everything in a playthrough, maybe just enough to miss a chunk if you were busy making other choices, but not enough to have a radically different experience the second time around, then playing it twice would just be pushing through a lot of the same things you’ve already done. Micro changes in context, but macro similarities in activity. If someone wants to see everything in there and they still want the goodie gumdrops school prefect ending, they’re being more generous to their own time and patience than they’re limiting their appreciation of art.

I respect people’s intelligence enough to believe they can be placed in a scene where the cost will be having to spend a lot of time they don’t want to spare, and empathise how much that would weigh on a person who doesn’t have it, without themselves actually having to carry that burden in their own game.

Personally, I don’t have any desire to mod the game to give Coen’s family a bit more breathing room, because I’m happy to accept whatever narrative conclusion I’m given as the result of my actions. I like the idea that my one playthrough would be informed wholly from my decisions, good or bad, and presumably expertly paced around the amount of time the devs think a person can play the game without it overstaying its welcome. Anything I miss, well, it wasn’t meant to be.

The Blood of Dawnwalker - IGN First Exclusive Images

I am, however, willing to admit that my stance here comes with some baggage: I don’t really care that much about finishing games at all, at least when I’m not playing for review. I’ll often get very close to the end of a game and decide that I’ve seen enough of it. Star Wars: Zero Company has a very interesting take on the tactics genre and a few excellent surprises; I still can’t help but feel like I’ve experienced every possible combination of abilities it has available and I’m not really driven to repeat them. I’m a mechanics guy, not a story guy. If there were 100 possible endings, I’m never going to see 100 of them. Given that I will pay upwards of £60 for one weekend of a game I’ll get over without completing, I think anyone who would care to mod their ability to achieve a particular endings, or see more of a game’s story, inherently cares more about the experience than I do, rather than less.

This is beside my point, but it’s fun to think about: Why is narrative intent considered more sacred than aesthetic design? I’ll regularly watch clips of people playing Deadlock where characters have been modded to look like Lebron James in the Space Jam sequel. I couldn’t imagine anyone writing an op-ed to deride anyone doing it as straying outside of the game designer's artistic necessity.

I’ve entertained the argument for being against modding difficulty , that games in the Souls series are easier than they get credit for and they’re more about the determination to continue, which you’d be robbing yourself of by not giving it your all. Dawnwalker initially feels like we’re having the same conversation, but the alteration made by modders isn’t necessarily making the game easier so much as it’s making the game less restrictive .

The time limit might be the point of the game, but really the point of the game, like all the rest of them, is to have something to do while your mates are out of town and your partner is at a work thing. I just don’t think it’s that deep, and if it were that deep, I think it’s as deep as doing a YouTube search for an ending you didn’t get, but you get to play a few extra hours of a video game you really like first.

Mat Jones is a Senior Social Producer for IGN based out of London, UK

articles.title: The Resident Evil Movie Understands Video Games Are Ridiculous, and That's Why It's Great - IGN
articles.summary: Zach Cregger's Resident Evil movie understands that video games are ridiculous, and that's why it's great.Video games are ridiculous. The Resident Evil series is a perfect example of this. One moment you’re running in terror away from a comically oversized trench-coated tank of a man in a tiny hat; the next, you’re messing around with electronic chess pieces in order to open a door. These are completely alien situations that, somehow, these games make us feel compelled to navigate through rational thought. This is what Zach Cregger understands about Capcom’s genre-defining series so well. His Resident Evil movie knows that this is all ridiculous, and so the film has its lead, Brian, progress through its 90-minute rollercoaster just as we would if we had a controller in our hands. It’s a fantastic translation of the sensation that playing a survival horror game grants us, never forgetting to include every piece of glorious nonsense that comes with it.

articles.title: IGN's Top-Reviewed Horror Movies of 2026
articles.summary: 2026 has been a particularly strong year for horror, but some scares stand out from the pack. These are IGN's picks for the 10 best horror movies of the year so far.
articles.body:
We're big fans of horror here at IGN, so it’s been a blast to see so many fresh concepts and interesting adaptations hit the big (or small) screen in 2026. While we’ve yet to give a horror movie from this year a full 10/10, a solid spread of new movies, including box office hits and some lesser-known independent releases, have secured a place in our list of the top-reviewed movies of the year so far.

What exactly defines “horror” can always be debated, so we’ve included a mix of slashers, thrillers, and even some horror comedies. However you prefer to get your scares, there’s something worth watching on this list.

From IGN's Review: "Sam Raimi drives the survival thriller genre to some amazing and sadistically giddy ends, with Rachel McAdams and Dylan O’Brien along for the ride in the back seat cackling and stabbing each other the whole way through. Linda and Bradley’s ordeal creates immensely fertile ground for Raimi to interrogate the validity of first impressions with twists and turns of the plot and of various sharp objects that seldom tire. Sure, drag me to hell, but let's stop at this island on the way and have a freakin’ party with Linda and Bradley!" - Tom Jorgenson

From IGN's Review: "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma is as much Jane Schoenbrun again at their best as it sees them taking us in surprising new directions. It’s sexual, sincere, silly, and sweet all at once – an earnest exploration of desire that’s deeply, movingly personal. For all the ways it could lose people in its messiness, Schhoenbrun and their strong cast hold it all together, building to an ecstatic climax that will only make you wish you could come back for more." - Chase Hutchinson

From IGN's Review: "Director Nia DaCosta crafts a great follow-up to last year’s 28 Years Later that’s gory and thoughtful in equal measure. There’s a wit and humor at play in The Bone Temple that elevates, in all the right ways, the dramatic stakes of a zombie apocalypse working on its third decade, especially in Ralph Fiennes’ record collection (I’d give the film a 666 if IGN would let me). While it might not be the best place to start watching the 28 Later franchise for the uninitiated, the creative force driving the series’ future have two solid movies as the foundation for whatever comes next." - Clint Gage

From IGN's Review: "They Will Kill You is another winner from director Kirill Sokolov that shows Zazie Beetz has all the chops to be an action star in her own right. With great stunt choreography and camerawork, it’s a shining example of how modern action ought to be constructed. With a supernatural, satanic twist that it fully capitalizes on, it’s a gonzo, gruesome, gutsy little gem." - Chase Hutchinson

From IGN's Review: "The question of how and why you would even attempt to remake Faces of Death is given a compelling answer in this new remake. Using a postmodern meta take on both the original film and how it was perceived, the movie reflects a world where rather than hunting down a specific VHS tape to see people supposedly really die, you can now find exactly that type of content immediately by simply going on the internet…and that is far from a comforting thought!" - Eric Goldman

From IGN's Review: "Thanks to fantastic turns by Michael Johnston and Inde Navarrette, you'll be addicted to this sour Valentine's Day counterprogramming. The film plays on familiar romance and monkey's paw tropes, turning a wish against the wishee, but Barker's execution takes things to the next level. In the film's simplicity lay the chance to go for broke, putting all efforts into the lengths Nikki is willing to go for her beloved." - Matt Donato

From IGN's Review: "Backrooms expertly expands on the conceptual groundwork of the YouTube series with smart visual composition, beautifully terrifying production design, a complex protagonist, and a return to Kane Parsons’ roots of computer generated sequences that pack a serious punch. The film also opens the doors to some compelling pathways to deepen the lore even more, if newcomers are willing to meet the film on its level, where it isn’t going to spoon-feed anyone." - Lex Briscusco

From IGN's Review: "Adrian Chiarella’s Leviticus is an involving, meaningful, and legitimately creepy horror movie. Chiarella’s story about gay youth being punished for simply being the way they are is emotional and thoughtful while also simply working well as a horror story, blending the real-life prejudices that inspired it with the supernatural curse laid upon its characters in a highly effective manner." - Eric Goldman

From IGN's Review: "It Ends manages to be both creepy and amusing thanks to its likable cast and filmmaker Alexander Ullom’s ability to exploit minimal resources to maximum effect. This is a movie that takes place in a car. In the woods. That’s it! And yet it’s scary, the characters really grow on you, and it also poses some self-aware and probing questions that will at the very least have you putting on the Talking Heads’ album Little Creatures when you’re done." - Scott Collura

From IGN's Review: "With a laser focus on putting its hero through the worst night of his life, Resident Evil is a simple and exciting survival horror story that benefits greatly from Zach Cregger’s sensibilities. Austin Abrams is exceedingly charming as the woefully outmatched medical courier Bryan as he’s dragged through a hellish coterie of well-realized mutants and monsters by Cregger, whose good eye for creature effects, mounting dread, and signature humor all leave Resident Evil feeling very well represented." - Tom Jorgenson

Blythe (she/her) is an Audience Development Coordinator at IGN who spends way too much time in character customization screens and tracking down collectibles.

articles.title: The Batman Part 2 Director Reveals New Image Seemingly Set in a Snowy Gotham Junkyard
articles.summary: The Batman Part 2 director Matt Reeves has done his part to celebrate Batman Day by sharing a new image from the movie.
articles.body:
The Batman Part 2 director Matt Reeves has done his part to celebrate Batman Day by sharing a new image from the movie.

Another September means another Batman Day, and while we're still years away from seeing Robert Pattinson reprise his role as the Caped Crusader, that isn't stopping DC Studios from celebrating. Reeves did his part to get in on the festivities by ending another months-long social media hiatus with an ominous picture from the set of The Batman Part 2 in London.

If you've seen 2022's The Batman, you'll be happy to know even this early image from the movie teases a film that will feel right at home in the saga. What we see here appears to be the back of Pattinson's Bruce Wayne as he looks ahead into what seems to be a forest-y area. We can only really see his silhouette, but it's at least yet another confirmation that The Batman Part 2 will take place in and around the snow.

"Happy Batman Day to everyone from London!" Reeves said in his post.

Is there much we can confidently say this image reveals about the plot of Reeves' new movie? Well, no, but fans are still using the holiday as an opportunity to comb through every pixel of The Batman Part 2 image in hopes of deciphering any details about its plot and characters.

One rumored villain that has stuck in the years it's taken to get The Batman sequel into theaters revolves around Gotham's secret collection of evil elites, The Court of Owls. Recently leaked set photos only stoked those flames , with fans saying that, even if there aren't any owls to be found in the new set image, they're still looking for them.

Another theory circling the new Batman image has fans arguing about the area the Dark Knight is surrounded by. Some think trees, others see smoke, and some see cars. Popular The Batman Part 2 fan account @TheBatmanSagaNW believes the setting we see here is a junkyard filled with piled-up vehicles. If that's true, it could potentially be linked to another previous rumor regarding a junkyard that will show up in the movie. IGN tweaked the image's brightness and was able to make out a location that does resemble what we'd imagine a snowy Gotham junkyard to look like.

Oh my god this shot confirms that the Junkyard set is real!!! 🦇 pic.twitter.com/R9Qxj3iT1L — The Batman Saga News (@TheBatmanSagaNW) September 19, 2026

Oh my god this shot confirms that the Junkyard set is real!!! 🦇 pic.twitter.com/R9Qxj3iT1L

ITS THE JUNKYARD HES IN THE JUNKYARD — Flo (@FloHasReturned) September 19, 2026

It's hard to make too much out right now, and with nearly a year and a half to go before the film's release and no sign of any trailers, it will likely be a while before we learn how Reeves' set image fits into place. Following some delays, The Batman Part 2 is currently scheduled to swoop into theaters February 18, 2028.

articles.title: We Ranked The 10 Best Eevee Pokémon Cards of All Time
articles.summary: We've ranked the 10 best Eevee Pokémon cards of all time, from priceless Japanese trophy promos to iconic vintage classics and modern chase cards.
articles.body:
If you know one thing about me, it’s that I love Eevee.

Between a shelf overflowing with a collection of over 100 Eevee plushies and my ongoing quest to complete an ultimate Eevee Master Set binder (collecting every single variant, promo, and English card ever printed for our favorite fluffball), this Pokémon is my number one.

30th Celebration 2-Pack Blister - ME: 30th Celebration

Eevee - 173 - SV: Scarlet & Violet Promo Cards (SVP)

Eevee (Illustration Rare) — SV06: Twilight Masquerade #188/167

Eevee & Snorlax-GX — Sun & Moon: Team Up #120/181

So with the 30th Celebration expansion release and Eeveelution chase cards dominating the market, what better time to settle this once and for all: which is the best Eevee card of all time? And I mean Eevee - pure, unevolved, Normal-type Eevee.

No disrespect to the Eeveelutions, but if we let them on this list, we all know Moonbreon would shoot to number one quicker than we can shuffle a deck.

Before we jump in, for those after 30th Celebration boosters, our best suggestion right now is to request an invite from Amazon for the ETB at least , priced much more reasonably compared to other retailers. Invites will be sent out soon!

10. Eevee — Pokémon TCG: 30th Celebration 2-Pack Blister Promo

​Kicking off our list at number ten is the brand-new promo dropping as part of the 30th Anniversary celebration, illustrated by Haru Akasaka.

This compact blister pack bundles two 30th Celebration booster packs, a plastic commemorative coin, and a guaranteed, absolutely adorable foil Eevee promo for $9.99.

It’s a very cute card, and an accessible pickup for anyone looking to join the anniversary hype while adding a fresh Eevee promo to their collection.

I have a soft spot for this card - this is the classic card that started my personal Eevee master collection after a friend picked it up for me at Christmas. Illustrated by legendary artist Kagemaru Himeno, this original 1999 Jungle common was one of the first cards I collected as a kid, and I know I’m not the only one. While a raw Jungle copy will only set you back a few bucks today, it served as the original artwork base for the famous 2002 Legendary Collection Reverse Holo Fireworks variant (#74/110)—a pristine PSA 10 copy of which recently made history by selling for a staggering $66,000 at auction!

Hailing from the beloved 2003 Skyridge expansion—the final e-Reader set printed by Wizards of the Coast—this card features artist Sumiyoshi Kizuki's signature patch-style of art. I love the 3D fabric effect of this card, it really stands out. Its low print run and iconic e-Series frame make raw copies command around $51.45 on the secondary market.

​7. Eevee (Holo Promo) — 2000 Japanese Pokémon Fan Club Promo

This is one of the most prestigious trophy cards in the entire Eevee TCG history. Its rarity bumps it up a few spots in this list, but it’s mainly made it thanks to its cheeky wink. Originally awarded to members of the Japanese Pokémon Fan Club who accumulated 500 total GET Points through magazine activities and events in 2000, this holy grail card features a gorgeous rainbow foil finish and unique expansion stamp. Because of its extreme rarity, copies of this card can fetch between $2,200.00 – $2,800.00 on major auction sites.

​6. Eevee (Illustration Rare) — SV: Scarlet & Violet Promo #173

​Illustrated by Atsushi Furusawa, this promo card captures Eevee lounging lazily on a comfy looking cushion. I love this card because it’s the spitting image of when my cats are comfy as heck, with their whole tummy out. With the sun streaming through the window, it makes me wish I could live the life of a spoiled Eevee. Sitting right around $13 on TCGplayer, it is an absolute steal for any Eevee fan.

5. Eevee & Snorlax-GX — Sun & Moon: Team Up #120/181

This is the legendary tag team from Sun & Moon: Team Up. Illustrated by the iconic Mitsuhiro Arita, this card shows a tiny Eevee happily perched on top of a massive, sleeping Snorlax's belly. A hallmark of TCG history, it comfortably goes for around $91 on TCGplayer.

4. Eevee-GX — SM Black Star Promos #SM233

Affectionately called Eevee Chungus in fan communities, this card cracks me up every time I see it. The only card illustrated by popular Japanese manga artist and animator Q-rais, this SM Black Star Promo features a delightfully chunky, wide-eyed Eevee drawn in Q-rais’s signature quirky, webcomic art style. Released as part of the Eevee-GX Box, its unique aesthetic has made it a massive cult favorite among collectors, pushing its price to over $134 on TCGplayer.

​3. Eevee ex (Special Illustration Rare) — SV: Prismatic Evolutions #167/131

The cover star of the incredibly popular Prismatic Evolutions, this Eevee, illustrated by Sowsow, is one of the top chase cards in the Prismatic Evolutions expansion. this Special Illustration Rare shows Eevee ex surrounded by colorful, glowing elemental crystals that subtly hint at all eight of its possible evolution paths. It’s a breathtaking card, along with its breathtaking price - sitting near $181.

Big stepper - this Eevee card, illustrated by You Iribi, is a steal at $8.35 on TCGplayer. If you place this Eevee V card side-by-side with the Pikachu V (#SWSH285) promo card (released in the Crown Zenith Special Collections), the background graphics and vibrant rainbow artwork align to form a single, continuous connecting panorama.

1. Eevee (Illustration Rare) — SV06: Twilight Masquerade #188/167

What’s better than one Eevee? Eight Eevees! Narumi Sato’s beloved Twilight Masquerade hit is a masterpiece in domestic chaos. If I lived in the mysterious world of Pokémon, I feel like this is an insight into my life. This mischievous pack of Eevee completely taking over a living room—knocking over pillows, climbing furniture, and causing adorable mayhem. It quickly became one of the most sought-after chase cards in the Scarlet & Violet block, steadily holding a $93 market value.

Sara Heritage is a freelance journalist for IGN, specialising in Pokémon TCG. When she's not gaming, you’ll probably find her building yet another LEGO set she absolutely did not need, or chaining ranked matches in Pokémon Champions.

articles.title: Insomniac Says Marvel's Wolverine Uses No Generative AI After Fans Spot Strange Signs in-Game
articles.summary: Insomniac Games has stepped in to confirm Marvel's Wolverine contains no generative AI after a few bizarre in-game signs raised eyebrows on social media.
articles.body:
Insomniac Games has stepped in to confirm Marvel's Wolverine contains no generative AI after a few bizarre in-game signs raised eyebrows on social media.

The hubbub surrounding the new PlayStation 5 exclusive's latest controversial moment kicked off when TikToker SmoothMango shared a video of their findings online (via Kotaku ). Their minute-long clip focused on not one but two different bathroom signs that featured melted-together figures that look not unlike the kind of AI-generated assets audiences have attempted to train themselves to watch for.

"Folks, that looks AI-generated," SmoothMango said. "I am trying to think of a way to describe this that is not AI generation because there's no way it's a bathroom for mutants. That looks supremely sus."

At least as it's presented here, the bathroom signs certainly seem odd. With fear surrounding AI at an all-time high, fans latched onto the clip, concerned that Insomniac had used the controversial technology to help build Marvel's Wolverine.

The glitchy bathroom signs then, of course, found their way over to X/Twitter, where user Rock Solid shared images from the video. Fans again swarmed out of fear, but Insomniac has since said its Wolverine game doesn't feature a drop of genAI.

The developer's director of community and marketing, James Stevenson, replied to the X post in question to clear the air. He said "a UV map bug" is behind the strange bathroom signs, promising that Insomniac is currently working on a fix that should address any similar instances of glitchy visuals. For those who still had question marks above their heads, Stevenson was more direct: "There are no AI-generated assets in Marvel's Wolverine."

No. This is a UV map bug and we have a fix coming. There are no AI generated assets in Marvel’s Wolverine. — James Stevenson (@JamesStevenson) September 18, 2026

No. This is a UV map bug and we have a fix coming. There are no AI generated assets in Marvel’s Wolverine.

When Insomniac will deploy the fix remains unclear, but those worried the bathroom image may be a sign the developer used genAI for its new PS5 game can at least rest easy. It's the conclusion to yet another speed bump for the Wolverine game just days following its September 15 launch.

The first and, perhaps, most visible controversy arrived in the form of Logan's Scent Trails, which fans online had not-so-lovingly dubbed "fart gas." Thankfully, a small fix for that arrived just yesterday, with Insomniac promising to investigate a toggle option for the tracking feature as post-launch work continues. While one issue is stamped out, others are still finding reasons to be upset with the game's linear story .

Despite the backlash online , Marvel's Wolverine showed up with a seemingly strong start in terms of sales . IGN gave Insomniac's latest a 6/10 review , saying that its "slick and satisfying combat wears thin well before its conclusion, so much so that even its strong character work can't quite save it from being anything more than okay."

articles.title: The Last of Us Director Apologizes to God of War Laufey Devs After Calling Recent AAA Games 'Boring'
articles.summary: The Last of Us game director Bruce Straley has apologized to the God of War Laufey team after his comments about modern AAA games brought "uninvited and unnecessary negative attention."
articles.body:
The Last of Us game director Bruce Straley has apologized to the God of War Laufey team after his comments about modern AAA games brought "uninvited and unnecessary negative attention."

The comments in question surfaced as part of a recently published piece by Edge magazine and saw the former Naughty Dog developer tackling the state of AAA gaming and game development. Straley initially said with a laugh that he thinks "the verbs and experiences we're delivering in the triple-A space are… I wanna say boring," before bringing God of War Laufey into the equation.

"God of War Laufey, I look at that game, and every pixel is mindblowing," he said to Edge. "The amount of work and skill that's gone into every single frame… I've made those kinds of games, and I'm still blown away. But when I actually look at what you're doing in the game? I'm not excited. And that's nothing against the God of War team. Just, across the board in triple-A, it feels like there’s no opportunity to inject fresh, innovative ideas."

The Last of Us has certainly had its influence on the state of big-budget games, so it was no surprise to see social media light up with reactions to Straley's thoughts. The former Naughty Dog lead then followed up the commotion with a thread of posts on X/Twitter , taking the opportunity to elaborate on his perspective on where the industry is at and where it's heading.

"I want to apologize to the Laufey team for dragging you all into this uninvited and unnecessary negative attention," he said. "I was trying to illustrate an industry concern and my mistake of naming your game is being used out of context and for clickbait. You don’t need this. I’m sorry.

"A journo asked me about the state of our industry. I mentioned a few concerns. One being the lack of innovation & risks taken in the AAA space. Though this isn’t the team’s fault! My fear is that our player base is getting tired of playing the same verbs for the last 20 years.

I want to apologize to the Laufey team for dragging you all into this uninvited & unnecessary negative attention. I was trying to illustrate an industry concern & my mistake of naming your game is being used out of context & for clickbait. You don’t need this. I’m sorry. 🧵 pic.twitter.com/Ri2KgfJ4yY — Bruce Straley (@bruce_straley) September 18, 2026

I want to apologize to the Laufey team for dragging you all into this uninvited & unnecessary negative attention. I was trying to illustrate an industry concern & my mistake of naming your game is being used out of context & for clickbait. You don’t need this. I’m sorry. 🧵 pic.twitter.com/Ri2KgfJ4yY

"My hypothesis: Our medium is unique because players are DOING a thing. There’s a different physiological response than viewers who just WATCH a movie. This requires us creators to continue to push and create new experiences, or we run the risk of diminishing players’ dopamine."

Straley then pointed to Half-Life 2, Gears of War, BioShock, Uncharted 2, and The Last of Us as a string of games that helped "set the 'modern AAA' mold," saying that each title felt like it wanted to bring new experiences to the space. He then clarified that this part of the conversation "is only one side of my concerns."

"Unfortunately the platforms that need to bring stability have eroded the ability to innovate," he continued. "The quest for [games as a service] and wanting to recreate the next Overwatch, Fortnite, Roblox, etc. is not a viable strategy and frankly shows these 'industry leaders' don't know their own brand.

"Hot take: There's a lack of good leadership, clear direction, and conviction from the people at the top, in charge of the money. (Money = stability) I believe if they understand their brand, they could have honest, inspiring conversations with creators to steer our medium to innovate."

Straley left The Last of Us studio after 18 years in September 2017. He went on to help start new game studio Wildflower Interactive in 2022 and is currently working on a new game called Coven of the Chicken Foot .

"ANYWAY… blah blah blah. I have thoughts about what's wrong and the possible serious harm done to our industry and how we might be able to fix it. But in trying to have a thoughtful conversation I stuck my foot in my mouth and mentioned Laufey, and that was my mistake. FIN (for now)."

God of War Laufey was announced as the next chapter in Santa Monica Studio's mythology-hopping action-game saga during a PlayStation State of Play presentation in June of this year. Although it's set to offer a different perspective on the universe with a story told through the eyes of Deborah Ann Woll's all-powerful Faye, it's already faced its fair share of pushback online . While some have expressed concern about playing any character other than Kratos, the studio has promised time and time again that the Ghost of Sparta will return.

God of War Laufey director Ariel Lawrence has asked skeptical fans to give Faye's story a chance ahead of its February 16, 2027 launch . While we wait to see more about how it connects to Santa Monica's gaming universe, you can read why one IGN writer felt that what we've seen so far looks too similar to Kratos' Norse saga .

articles.title: Big Bang Theory Spinoff Features Surprise Live-Action Cameos from The Flash and Mr. Freeze
articles.summary: Big Bang Theory spinoff Stuart Fails to Save the Universe featured a surprise fight between a live-action Flash and Mr. Freeze, but the show's creators originally wanted a different DC hero cameo.
articles.body:
Big Bang Theory spinoff Stuart Fails to Save the Universe featured a surprise fight between a live-action Flash and Mr. Freeze, but the show's creators originally wanted a different DC hero cameo.

Fans of the sci-fi comedy offshoot may have been surprised to see it dive headfirst into comic book crossover territory when Season 1 Episode 9 premiered earlier this week. The episode saw Stuart Bloom and his universe-traveling companions plopped into a Gotham City come to life, with things quickly taking a turn when none other than classic Batman villain Mr. Freeze (played here by Eric Allan Kramer) shows up.

TV show budgets aside, this is a full-on live-action take on Victor Fries that shoots killer icicles, builds giant ice walls, and even tries to kill Stuart with a giant icy bowling ball. DC fans found even more to recognize when a live-action version of Jay Garrick's Flash (played by Andy Ridings) ran in to save the day – and deliver a few one-liners.

The Flash has officially appeared in live action in ‘The Big Bang Theory’ Stuart spinoff show. pic.twitter.com/UnfelkJErE — DCU Brief (@DCUBrief) September 18, 2026

The Flash has officially appeared in live action in ‘The Big Bang Theory’ Stuart spinoff show. pic.twitter.com/UnfelkJErE

Stuart Fails to Save the Universe packed in the references, with there even being a mention that Golden Age Flash should probably be fighting someone like Captain Cold instead of Mr. Freeze. It was enough to get tongues wagging on social media, with fans mostly just happy to see any live-action Flash for the first time since Ezra Miller played Barry Allen in 2023's universe-ending standalone film .

"Why is the costume good???" one fan said .

"The clash of the bulky mechanic Mr. Freeze and the vibrant spandex on Flash? Oh yeah, that’s what it’s all about," another said .

As much of a splash as The Flash vs. Mr. Freeze made, this specific matchup wasn't the original plan. Stuart Fails to Save the Universe co-creator Zak Penn told Deadline that the episode's title, "Spoiler: We Couldn't Get Green Lantern," was more than just a gag. You can probably guess why Hal Jordan or John Stewart didn't show up.

"They told us we couldn’t have him because of [HBO’s live-action series] Lanterns , which I understood," Penn said. "Chuck [Lorre] was a little grumbly about it, but Bill and I pointed out to him that Flash was actually perfect. If we needed something that’s going from dimension to dimension, Flash worked even better than Green Lantern."

Lanterns, of course, is very much still on the air, so bringing any of its characters – and even potentially its actors – could have been pretty confusing. The DCU show has so far received praise for its grounded approach to two classic Green Lanterns, and it's clear the Big Bang Theory spinoff was going for something a little more tongue-in-cheek.

Stuart Fails to Save the Universe is also in the midst of its first season, which will conclude when episode 10 premieres next week. The DCU is currently without a live-action Flash or Mr. Freeze, but Lanterns will continue to construct its Hal and John when its next episode arrives tomorrow , September 20, 2026.

articles.title: Bristol Harbour clean-up group celebrates 10 years of odd finds
articles.summary: The group is marking a decade of fishing everything from an inflatable doll to a Nintendo out of the harbour.
articles.body:
A voluntary clean-up group is marking a decade of finding unusual items in Bristol Harbour, ranging from an inflatable doll to a Nintendo Switch.

Clean Up Bristol Harbour was launched in September 2016 in a bid to remove plastic pollution from in and around Bristol's waterways.

The group has fished out some unusual items from the harbour in the past 10 years, including a message in a bottle containing a note in Spanish, a kettle, tennis balls, glasses and single shoes as well as the inflatable doll and Nintendo Switch.

"You never quite know what you're going to pull out of Bristol Harbour," said founder and Bristol resident Chloe Juyon.

"Some of the things we've found over the years have definitely made us laugh but there is a serious point behind it.

"So much floating rubbish simply can't be reached from the harbourside.

"Getting volunteers onto the water was always a big part of what I wanted Clean Up Bristol Harbour to become."

However, the future of the project remains uncertain because funding was coming to an end, Juyon said.

Juyon founded the group after she was struck by the amount of rubbish floating around her boat while she was coxing on the River Avon at high tide.

The group has since been taken on by adventure sports centre All Aboard Watersports.

During recorded monitoring between 2021 and 2023, some 236 volunteers removed more than 880kg (1940lb) of waste from Bristol Harbour with almost 390kg (859lbs) sent for recycling.

Nipple tattooist 'frustrated' by online censorship

Dealer jailed for firearms and drug offences

'Helping people with music is my mission'

Much of the rubbish includes everyday waste, such as plastic packaging, bottles, cans, polystyrene and takeaway rubbish.

But over the years, volunteers have fished out some unusual items, such as a Nespresso capsules, alcohol bottles, plastic cones, clothing - including thermals still in their packaging - and even a packet of butcher's tripe mix.

One particularly unusual find was a Marathon-branded chocolate wrapper - the UK name for Snickers until 1990 - found during a clean-up several years ago.

Reflecting on the anniversary, Juyon said: "There were just five of us at that first clean-up in 2016.

"I stepped away from running the project several years ago, so seeing it reach its tenth birthday is quite amazing.

"For me, it really demonstrates the power of community."

To mark the 10th anniversary, the group will hold a community clean-up event later to mark World Cleanup Day.

Members of the public can take part in a self-guided litter pick from 10:00 to 12:00 BST, either on foot around the harbourside or using their own craft.

With its current funding coming to an end, All Aboard Watersports has launched a Crowdfunder bid aiming to raise an initial £5,000 to help continue the project.

Charley Peak-Payne, from All Aboard Watersports, said having a clean harbour has had a positive impact on people who use the harbourside for waters sports and boating.

"The direct effect it has had on wildlife has been a gradual but noticeable change," he said.

"The water that they are swimming in is considerably cleaner - to the point that we are now running swimming events in the harbour too, something that due to pollution would never have happened 10 years ago."
